html:
The Lewis and Clark Expedition was the United States Army party, the Corps of Discovery, that crossed the American West to the Pacific and back between 1804 and 1806. President Thomas Jefferson sent it to explore the lands of the Louisiana Purchase, look for a water route to the Pacific, and tell the nations it met that they now lived under the United States.

Captain Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led about thirty men up the Missouri from near St. Louis in May 1804. On the way:

  • In 1804 they held their first council with Native leaders, Otoe and Missouria chiefs, and met the Yankton.
  • They spent the winter of 1804 to 1805 with the Mandan and Hidatsa, where they took on Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, and her French husband as interpreters.
  • In 1805 her people, the Lemhi Shoshone, sold them horses to cross the Rockies, and the Nez Perce fed them and kept their horses.
  • They reached the Pacific in November 1805 and wintered at Fort Clatsop near the mouth of the Columbia, among the Clatsop and Chinook.

Only one man died, probably of appendicitis. The journals, maps and specimens they brought back opened the way for fur traders, settlers and the US claim to Oregon, and so for the loss of land that followed for the nations they had met.
